title: Week 1
text:
Summary
This week was an introduction to remote sensing and Earth observation (EO). The core idea is simple: sensors on satellites measure electromagnetic radiation (EMR) that bounces off the Earth’s surface, and we use that signal to understand what is on the ground. Passive sensors rely on sunlight, so they only work during the day and struggle with cloud cover. Active sensors like SAR send out their own microwave pulses, which means they can see through clouds and work at night (kerle2004?; butcher2016?).
One thing that clicked for me is why the sky is blue. Short blue wavelengths get scattered much more easily by atmospheric particles (Rayleigh scattering), while longer red wavelengths pass through. This same scattering is also why satellite images can look hazy, and why we need atmospheric correction. Sensors can only pick up signals within certain “atmospheric windows” where water vapour, ozone, and CO2 do not absorb the radiation (jensen2016?).
When choosing a sensor, there are four resolutions to think about: spatial (pixel size, e.g. 10 m for Sentinel-2 vs 30 m for Landsat), spectral (how many bands the sensor records), temporal (how often the satellite revisits), and radiometric (how sensitive the sensor is to small differences in energy). In general, you cannot have everything. Higher spatial resolution usually means lower temporal frequency.
In the practical I used SNAP to look at Sentinel-2 imagery of West London and Landsat 8 imagery of Cape Town. The true colour composite (red, green, blue bands) looks like a normal photograph. The false colour composite puts near-infrared in the red channel, which makes vegetation appear bright red because of the strong NIR reflectance at the “red edge”. Comparing the two sensors side by side, I could see that Sentinel-2’s 10 m pixels pick up individual parks and street trees, while Landsat’s 30 m pixels blur small green patches into the surrounding buildings.
Something useful I learned in SNAP is that histogram stretching only changes how the image looks on screen. It does not change the actual pixel values. So a nice-looking image is not necessarily better data (jensen2016?).
I also ran a Tasseled Cap Transformation on the Landsat data using the coefficients from Baig et al. (baig2014?). This reduces the spectral bands into three components: Brightness (built surfaces and bare soil), Greenness (vegetation), and Wetness (moisture). It is a useful way to compress the information into something more interpretable than raw bands.
Finally, I extracted spectral values from four land cover types (water, vegetation, urban, bare soil) using R to compare their signatures:
Code
library(terra)
library(tidyverse)

# Stack Landsat 8 SR bands B1-B7 and extract by land cover buffers
sr <- rast(list.files("Landsat/", pattern = "_SR_B[1-7]\\.TIF$",
                       full.names = TRUE))
# Create sample buffers for water, vegetation, urban, bare soil
# Extract pixel values per buffer, compute mean and SD per band
# Plot spectral profiles with error bars
The results match what the lecture described. Water absorbs almost everything and stays flat and low. Vegetation has the expected red edge jump from red to NIR. Bare soil reflects broadly. Urban areas sit somewhere in the middle with a fairly flat curve. It is one thing to hear about spectral signatures in a lecture, but seeing them come out of real data makes the concept much more concrete.

One area where this week’s content directly applies is urban greenness mapping. Robinson et al. (robinson2022?) calculated NDVI from Sentinel-2 across Great Britain and found that more deprived neighbourhoods tend to have less green cover. Their approach works because vegetation reflects strongly in near-infrared, so NDVI can separate green surfaces from buildings and roads. But even at 10 m, individual street trees or small gardens can get mixed into a single pixel, and the authors note that NDVI cannot tell the difference between tree canopy and grass, which provide quite different benefits.
Venter et al. (venter2020?) took this further in Oslo by combining Sentinel-2 NDVI with Landsat surface temperature data. They found that greener neighbourhoods were 2 to 3 degrees cooler in summer, and that lower-income areas tended to miss out on this cooling effect. What I found interesting is how they used the strengths of each sensor together: Sentinel for vegetation detail, Landsat for thermal data. The main limitation was cloud. Over five summers, they could only use 15 to 20 clear scenes.
On the thermal side, Deilami et al. (deilami2018?) reviewed 75 urban heat island studies and pointed out that most of them rely on a single Landsat image, which only captures mid-morning temperature on one day. This introduces obvious bias. Multi-date composites help, but they average across different weather conditions. For somewhere like West London, this means any heat analysis should use multiple years of data and ideally be checked against ground-level temperature records (majorsu?).



Proposed workflow linking Sentinel-2 greenness and Landsat thermal data

title: Week 1
text:
Reflection
Before this week I basically thought of satellite images as photos. Now I understand they are measurements of reflected energy at different wavelengths, and that what you see on screen depends on which bands you display and how you stretch the histogram. It sounds obvious when I write it down, but it was a genuine shift in how I think about the data.
SNAP was not the most pleasant software to use. The interface is clunky and the Sentinel file structure is confusing. But I do see why we used it: loading Sentinel-2 and Landsat side by side made the difference between 10 m and 30 m resolution real. I could zoom into a park and see trees in Sentinel that were just a blur in Landsat. That is harder to appreciate from a textbook.
The thing I keep coming back to from the readings is the gap between what satellites can measure and what a city council actually needs to make decisions. NDVI can show which neighbourhoods lack green cover, but planting trees also requires knowing who owns the land, what the soil is like, and what residents want. Remote sensing gives useful evidence, but it is not the whole answer (londone?). I want to keep thinking about this as we go through the module. For next week I plan to set up the Quarto portfolio and make sure everything is version-controlled properly.

title: Week 3
text:
Summary
This week focused on image corrections and image enhancement for remote sensing analysis. The lecture explained why raw pixel values are not stable across space and time. Geometric correction aligns an image to the ground so that each pixel is in the right place. This can involve ground control points, a transformation model, and resampling to a common grid (jensen2016?). Atmospheric correction reduces scattering and absorption so values are closer to surface reflectance (radiativ2013?). This supports fair comparison across dates and sensors and helps change analysis. The lecture also introduced analysis ready data, where key corrections are already applied, but the user still needs to understand what the product includes and what limits remain (ceosana?).
In the practical I used Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 surface reflectance for Cape Town (landsat2022?). I loaded only the surface reflectance bands and clipped them to my study area polygon. My shapefile had a missing coordinate system, so I assigned WGS84 and then transformed it to the Landsat projection before crop and mask. After clipping I created several enhancement layers. I calculated NDVI from the red and near infrared bands to describe vegetation activity (jensen2016?). The NDVI map shows higher values in the mountain and green areas and lower values over water and dense built surfaces.
I then applied a vegetation mask using an NDVI threshold of 0.2 to separate likely vegetation from other land covers. This mask is simple and fast, but it can include false positives where soil is bright or where shadows change the index (jensen2016?).
Next I tested spatial filtering on the red band. A low pass 3 by 3 mean filter reduced local noise and made broad patterns clearer. A high pass Laplacian filter highlighted edges, which made coastlines and sharp land cover boundaries more visible.
I also computed a texture proxy using a 7 by 7 local standard deviation. This layer emphasised heterogeneous urban fabric and mixed surfaces. Finally I fused the surface reflectance bands with the texture layer and ran PCA. The PCA composite increased contrast between major surface types and showed that combining spectral and spatial features can reveal structure that is not clear in one band.

title: Week 3
text:
Applications
Corrections matter when a study compares images across time or across sensors. Atmospheric effects can shift reflectance values even if the surface is unchanged, so surface reflectance products are often preferred for monitoring vegetation, drought, or urban change (jensen2016?; landsat2024?). A Cape Town drought study used Landsat data with vegetation indices to map drought severity and its spatial pattern, which shows how corrected reflectance supports environmental analysis at city scale (orimoloye2019?). In practice, using an analysis ready product reduces processing time, but it does not remove the need for quality checks. Cloud, haze, and shadow still affect pixels, and each product has its own algorithm and quality masks. For mosaics or multi-scene analysis, consistent correction also helps to reduce seams and brightness jumps before compositing or further modelling.
Enhancement methods then turn corrected bands into features that match a research question. NDVI is a simple ratio that isolates vegetation signal and reduces some illumination effects, so it is widely used for mapping urban greenness and tracking stress. In my outputs, the NDVI and the vegetation mask provide a fast first separation between vegetated and non-vegetated surfaces, which could support later classification or sampling design. Spatial filters and texture measures add information about local structure. Edge filters can highlight roads, coastlines, and block boundaries, while local variability can separate smooth water from complex built surfaces. Urban land cover studies often combine spectral indices with extra features and tuned thresholds because cities mix materials within one pixel and create strong shadow effects (faridatul2018?). Data fusion extends this idea by combining sensors with different strengths. A review on multispectral and radar fusion shows that combining datasets can improve monitoring when optical data are limited by clouds and when structure information is needed (schultetobuhne2018?). My fused PCA step followed the same logic at a smaller scale by combining reflectance with a texture layer, then using PCA to compress the information into a few components that are easier to visualise and can be used as inputs for models (jensen2016?).

title: Week 3
text:
Reflection
This week helped me link theory about corrections with practical feature building. I now see surface reflectance as a foundation for most comparisons, but I also see the risk of treating it as a black box. For my Cape Town workflow, the first challenge was not an algorithm but metadata, because my study area file had no coordinate system. Fixing the coordinate system and matching projections was essential before any analysis. This reminds me that good results depend on simple checks such as coordinate reference systems, band names, and missing data.
The enhancement steps were fast to run, but they involve choices that affect meaning. An NDVI threshold of 0.2 is easy to explain, yet it is not universal and it can confuse sparse vegetation, bright soil, and shadow. Texture and filtering depend on window size. A 7 by 7 window shows broad heterogeneity but can miss small features, and larger windows increase computation. The high pass filter made boundaries clearer, but it also amplified noise, so it needs careful display scaling and may not be stable for quantitative use without normalisation.
Next I want to improve this workflow by using the Landsat quality masks to remove clouds and by testing how sensitive results are to threshold and window size (landsat2024?). I also want to connect these features to an outcome, such as a supervised land cover map or a change map, so that I can evaluate whether added features truly improve performance rather than just looking visually better.

title: Week 4&5
text:
Summary
This week focused on turning a city policy challenge into a measurable monitoring plan using Earth Observation. I selected London and the challenge of extreme heat risk that is uneven across neighbourhoods. Heat is not only a climate issue. It is also a public health and environmental justice issue because exposure and vulnerability can cluster in the same places. A practical policy response needs clear targets, clear responsibilities, and a way to measure change over time. In London, greening policy already exists through the London Plan and the Urban Greening Factor guidance, which asks major developments to treat greening as a core design element and to report a greening score. This creates a strong entry point for EO evidence because EO can measure where heat and greenness are high or low, and whether patterns shift after investment and planning decisions.
I propose a simple EO indicator set that can support both targeting and accountability. First, Land Surface Temperature from Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 can provide a consistent time series to map hot surfaces and to track change after interventions such as new tree cover, green roofs, and shade. The product is designed as a surface temperature science product with quality layers and consistent processing, which supports repeatable analysis across seasons and years. Second, greenness from Sentinel 2 Level 2A surface reflectance can be used to calculate NDVI as a transparent indicator of vegetation signal at high spatial detail. These two indicators allow a policy narrative that is easy to explain. Where surfaces are hottest and greenness is lowest, London can prioritise greening actions and cooling design, then monitor whether the gap closes over time.
This approach aligns with global agendas. SDG 11 calls for inclusive and resilient cities, SDG 13 focuses on climate action, SDG 3 links to health, and SDG 10 links to reducing inequality. EO is valuable here because it can provide comparable evidence for progress and for fairness, not only for average city outcomes but also for the distribution of benefits.

title: Week 4&5
text:
Applications
Earth observation can support routine policy tasks such as monitoring, targeting, and evaluation. Gerasopoulos et al. describe EO as a practical input to urban governance when data are timely, accessible, and connected to decision needs . My workflow follows this logic by choosing open satellite products and by defining clear outputs that match a policy question, where to act first for urban cooling and greening. Wellmann et al. also show that remote sensing can contribute to planning, but only when results are translated into planning language and linked to the policy cycle . This is why I frame outputs as priority zones and measurable indicators, not only as scientific maps. Kadhim et al. review urban sustainability applications and highlight the need to connect methods to real policy use .
Li et al. connect historical inequality, urban heat, and health outcomes with spatial models across multiple cities . It provides evidence that heat exposure reflects structural injustice, which supports an equity based policy framing. Yet studies like this can stop before the last step, the design of an implementable planning rule or investment plan. I use it as a warning that correlation is not enough for policy. Martinez and Labib add another warning. They show that NDVI is often treated as a direct measure of green exposure, but it can hide differences between trees, grass, and season . For policy, this means NDVI should be used with care, and ideally combined with tree canopy or land cover when the policy aim is shade and cooling.
To move from evidence to action, I align the workflow with a simple governance pathway. First, use heat hotspot and greenness deficit maps to select candidate priority areas. Second, connect these zones to specific instruments, minimum greening requirements for new development and targeted canopy programs for existing neighbourhoods . Third, monitor change each year with the same EO indicators, and report progress against SDG 11 targets and London Plan objectives. This creates a repeatable loop that supports transparency and learning, while keeping uncertainty explicit.

title: Week 4&5
text:
Reflection
This week helped me see the difference between a technical map and a policy tool. A policy tool needs a clear user, a clear decision point, and a clear statement of uncertainty . The biggest barrier is often not data access. It is skills, time, and coordination across teams. Planning teams, public health teams, and climate teams may use different standards and different timelines. EO products can also be challenged by cloud cover, mixed pixels, and the gap between land surface temperature and lived heat stress (jensen2016?). These issues can reduce trust if they are not communicated simply.
Fairness is not automatic in data driven policy. If the city targets only the hottest places, it may miss communities with high vulnerability but moderate heat. If it targets only the most deprived places, it may overlook extreme hotspots that create acute health risk. An equity approach should combine exposure and vulnerability, and it should be checked with local knowledge . This is where community engagement and local sensor data can improve the EO screening maps. It also links to the idea that city level strategies often fail at the local scale, unless they are tied to implementable rules and budgets .
For my own practice, I learned to design EO analysis around a policy workflow, not around a dataset. I will carry this into later work by defining indicators first, then choosing data that can be updated and explained. I also want to extend beyond NDVI by adding tree canopy and impervious surface, so the policy message is closer to shade, cooling, and access to green public space.

title: CASA0023 Learning Diary
text:
Remotely Sensing Cities and Environments

A weekly learning diary for CASA0023 at UCL, covering remote sensing theory, Earth observation applications, and geospatial data science.







Author: ZheXiang Zhou | Programme: MSc Urban Spatial Science, UCL CASA | Term 2, 2026



This book records what I learned each week, from electromagnetic radiation fundamentals to Google Earth Engine workflows, alongside reflections on how Earth observation data can support urban policy and environmental decisions.
Each entry follows three sections:

Summary: key concepts, practical outputs, and what I noticed along the way
Applications: how the methods appear in published research and policy
Reflection: personal takeaways and connections to wider practice
